Testimony ofSenator Anne Carney in support of
LD 1087, "An Act to Increase the State's Share of Major Capital School
Construction Costs," Before the Joint Standing Committee on Education and Cultural Aflairs
May 6, 2025
Senator Rafferty, Representative Murphy and esteemed members of the Education and Cultural
Affairs Committee, I am Senator Anne Carney, proudly representing Senate District 29, which includes South Portland, Cape Elizabeth and part of Scarborough. Today, I am pleased to testify as a Co-Sponsor of LD 1087, "An Act to Increase the State's Share of Major Capital School
Construction Costs."
One of the urgent issues affecting the communities I represent and many others across the state is the need to replace school buildings ---- and how to pay for this vital infrastructure. I've
sponsored a bill before the Appropriations and Financial Affairs Committee to authorize a bond that would help communities pay for school building projects. This bill would be another tool to maximize the State's ability to help fund school construction project throughout Maine.
Many Maine communities face a common issue -- deteriorating school buildings that no longer
provide a safe, healthy and appropriate learning environment. These school buildings have wide glass doors instead of locking vestibules; they have mold and aging heating systems, instead of
dry ceilings and cooling systems necessitated by the higher temperatures Maine now experiences
during the school year; and they have classrooms that cannot accommodate the educational services that some students need to succeed at school.
At the same time, many Maine municipalities have experienced unprecedented increases in
residential property values -- which is great if you are trying to sell your home but terrible if you
are a long-time resident who wants to remain in your community after retirement. In some
communities, declining commercial property values have exacerbated this situation.
Many people who have resided in Senate District 29 for decades worry that increasing property
taxes will force them to leave their beloved homes and neighborhoods. For communities that face major school construction projects, this is a difficult math problem, especially when you add
in the rising costs of labor and materials to the equation.

1

This bill would add another resource to help communities put together the financing they need to build a safe, healthy and modern learning environment. The current revolving school
construction fund provides great support, but can only fund a few projects. And that waitlist is
very long. This bill would help stretch the state's resources across more schools in more communities. In turn, taxpayers in more towns and cities would get help paying for these vital
new school buildings.
The provisions in this legislation would help to ensure the state funding is distributed more
equitably, as well. Specifically, school districts who receive greater funding from the State,
which tend to have less local capacity to pay, would be eligible for a greater share of construction funding from the state. School districts throughout our state need some help replacing deteriorating, unsafe schools. I
urge you to vote Ought to Pass on LD 1087, "An Act to Increase the State's Share of Major
Capital School Construction Costs."
Thank you for your time and consideration today. I am happy to answer any questions you may
have.

To: Honorable Members of the Education and Cultural Affairs Committee
From: Chris Record, Superintendent Cape Elizabeth School District
Re: Written Testimony on LD 1087, An Act An Act to Increase the State's Share of Major Capital School Construction Costs
Dear Honorable Senators and Representatives,
My name is Chris Record and I am the very proud Superintendent of the Cape Elizabeth School District. I am testifying as to the grave importance of increasing access to state funding for school construction projects throughout the state. Furthermore, I advocate strongly for changing the approach to allow for sharing the construction funds more broadly, so more communities can tackle their school construction needs.
During the 2017-2018 Rating Cycle, there were seventy-four (74) schools on the Schools Facilities Priorities list. However, only nine (9) school construction projects were awarded. Great news for those nine school districts and communities, but extremely difficult news for the remaining sixty-five (65) communities that were left to wait for the next school construction round or try to go it alone on the local level.

If the amount of school construction dollars and the model for determining who gets what amount remains the same, there will once again be a few winners and dozens and dozens of losers. As you are likely aware, there are ninety-six (96) schools that are currently being ranked through the school construction Rating Cycle conducted by Scott Brown and his MDOE team. I fear the same result will occur again with a fraction of the projects being funded by the state.
In Cape Elizabeth, we have tried the local approach by trying to pass two school construction referendums, in 2022 and 2024. Both would have required the construction costs to be paid entirely by the local taxpayers. We got close, as the 2024 referendum lost by just 166 votes.
Can you imagine this scenario instead, where the MDOE would have offered to fund the community of Cape Elizabeth 25% of the project construction costs? I believe in my heart and mind that the citizens of Cape Elizabeth want to support schools and having some portion of the project covered by state tax dollars would have led to a successful referendum. This is very likely true in multiple communities around the state.
Just imagine the positive impact for students, staff, and communities if suddenly twenty to thirty projects could be completed during the construction cycle. This would be a game changer for education in Maine.

In closing, we need more funding for school construction in Maine and we need a better way to distribute those funds to allow many more of the much needed projects to be completed. The investment in Maine kids and communities is well worth it.
10050692:
Testimony in Support of LD 1087: An Act to Increase the State's Share of Major Capital School Construction Costs
May 6, 2025
Dear Senator Rafferty, Representative Noonan Murphy and distinguished members of the Committee on Education and Cultural Affairs,
My name is Cynthia Voltz and I am Vice-Chair of the Cape Elizabeth School Board. I'm writing to express strong support for LD 1087.
The Cape Elizabeth School Department has made two recent efforts to address the condition of our aging school facilities through local referenda. In 2022, we proposed a project to replace both the elementary and middle schools. That initiative failed. In 2024, we brought forward a more modest plan to replace the middle school and renovate the elementary school--again, the measure did not pass.
Now, in 2025, we are preparing for a third attempt. On June 10, Cape Elizabeth voters will consider a revised proposal to replace the middle school and address critical needs at the elementary school. Despite multiple project revisions and careful cost reductions, we continue to face a familiar barrier: the total cost of the project will fall solely on local taxpayers.
I recognize that Cape Elizabeth is not alone in this challenge. Across Maine, many school departments are struggling to replace or repair outdated buildings while balancing the fiscal realities their communities face.
The current school construction funding model in Maine operates as an all-or-nothing system--either a project qualifies for 100% state funding or it receives nothing. Because of this, and because available state funds are limited, only a very small number of school construction projects are approved in any given funding cycle. This leaves the vast majority of school districts, like Cape Elizabeth, with no option but to pursue fully locally funded solutions, which often fail at the ballot box due to cost concerns.
LD 1087 offers a smarter approach. By allowing for partial state funding--at least 25%--more communities could move forward with essential school improvements, and the state's limited construction dollars could be distributed more equitably and effectively across Maine.
Thank you for your time and your continued commitment to public education.
Respectfully,
Cynthia Voltz Vice Chair, Cape Elizabeth School Board

Town of Cape Elizabeth
TO: Senator Joseph Rafferty, Representative Kelly Noonan Murphy (Co-Chairs) Members of the Committee on Education and Cultural Affairs
DATE: May 6, 2025 RE: LD 1087- An Act to Increase the State's Share of Major Capital School Construction Costs
Good afternoon, Senator Rafferty, Representative Murphy, and members of the committee. My name is Patrick Fox. I am the Town Manager in Cape Elizabeth and writing in support of LD 1087.
The Maine Department of Education has stated that the State bears the major financial burden of capital costs in most school units, providing an unprecedented $580 million since 2019 for school renovation and construction. However, the current "all or nothing" funding model for new schools means that very few communities actually benefit from this.
The $580 million allocated is enough to build approximately 7 new schools at $80 million each. While this is a windfall for these few, it leaves many communities waiting and detracts from districts' primary focus: education.
Communities face a difficult choice: allow their schools to deteriorate for years to move up the State funding list, or resort to a locally funded option when residents decide they've had enough. Locally funded projects can heavily impact the local property tax base and often lead to years of community division before approval.
I urge you to use bill LD 1087 to make the school construction funding work for everyone. Please consider revising the new school funding formula to leverage local dollars by distributing the next $580 million as 25% to 50% matching funds for new school construction. This approach could help construct 15 to 30 new schools. Communities currently facing 10% to 12% property tax increases for locally funded projects could see impacts reduced to 5% to 9% under a matching funds model. This significant shift would likely lead to projects being approved on the first referendum, avoiding prolonged and contentious community debates.
Let's adopt collaborative funding models to ensure that all our educational facilities are well-maintained, rather than creating a system of winners and losers.

Senator Rafferty, Representative Murphy, and members of the committee I am Penny Jordan, Chair of the Cape Elizabeth Town Council. I am submitting testimony in support of LD 1087 "An Act to Increase the State's Share of Major Capital School Construction Costs".

I want to say this a bill is long overdue as towns across Maine continue to grapple with aging schools. Action by the state to spread the dollars available for school projects across a multitude of towns is critical as communities face the ever-growing challenges of how to fund renovation or replacement to their aging infrastructure.

I am sure you hear from many communities about the financial challenges experienced to upgrade or replace their aging schools. Many of these schools were built to accommodate the baby boomers, some are even older.

In November 2022 a $115 million bond for new schools was voted down in Cape Elizabeth. In November 2024 a $94.7 million project was voted down. In both instances it was the resulting tax impact that was voiced as the cause. This bill would allow funding for a portion of a project and could result in projects moving forward and help lessen the impact on property owners.

In June Cape Elizabeth will vote for the third time to fund the construction of a new middle school and renovations to our elementary school at a cost of $89.5 million, resulting in a 12.3% tax increase. It would be ideal if there was a way to access funding to offset a portion of the cost and the resulting impact.

You often hear people say it's the teachers not the buildings that create a strong school system. In Support of LD 1048 "An Act to Increase the State's Share of Major Capital School Construction Costs"
Rebecca Millett, Cape Elizabeth
In its 2023 report to the Committee on Education and Cultural Affairs, the Maine Department of Education stated:
The need for enhanced school construction funding is great, as evidenced by applications for limited state funding in the previous cycles of the Major Capital School Construction Program. In 2010-2011, 71 schools applied for major capital construction projects and only 16 were selected for funding. In 2017-2018, the next rating cycle, 74 applications were submitted, with only seven projects funded. The next application cycle will be initiated in calendar year 2024. While many communities are applying for this funding, the amount of funding available is not sufficient to meet their needs. With an aging stock of school buildings throughout the state, we anticipate continued high demand for state support in shouldering the cost burdens of school renovation and new construction on local municipalities.
And the 2024 Report Card for Maine's Infrastructure estimates a $2.6 billion backlog in school construction.1
LD 1048 is a long overdue change in the way Maine addresses school construction. Currently only a lucky few receive 100% funding, leaving too many communities out to dry. And this is only going to be worse with skyrocketing costs while the debt limit is held constant. By capping how much a community receives in construction funding by the percentage amount of its EPS funding, we can free up more funds to help other communities faced with crumbling, dangerous and unhealthy buildings.
There never is a magic solution that will instantly address the whole problem. As policy makers, you can make changes that moves the dial in the right direction and LD 1048 will help open the door to a few more projects.
Please vote Ought to Pass and let's start opening the doors for more safe and healthy schools.
Thank you for your consideration.

TESTIMONY NEITHER FOR NOR AGAINST
L.D. 1087
AN ACT TO INCREASE THE STATE'S SHARE OF MAJOR CAPITAL SCHOOL CONSTRUCTION COSTS
May 6, 2025
Senator Rafferty, Representative Noonan Murphy, and esteemed members of the Education and Cultural Affairs Committee, I am Robbie Feinberg, the director of communications and government relations for Maine School Management Association, testifying on behalf of the legislative committees of the Maine School Superintendents Association and the Maine School Boards Association neither for nor against L.D. 1087, An Act to Increase the State's Share of Major Capital School Construction Costs.
Both superintendents and school boards support the broader goal of this bill - to adjust the current funding system for the Maine Capital School Construction Program, which currently operates in essentially an "all-ornothing" system: if a project is approved, the state covers nearly all the funding. Yet schools that do not make the list receive no financial assistance. They must either wait for the next funding round or fund construction themselves.
This has helped the few districts that do get a school built. But dozens and dozens of other districts are still waiting, with their school buildings getting older. Many superintendents feel this is inequitable, and requiring some sort of local contribution would be an effective strategy towards helping to spread state funding out and ultimately get more districts built.
The Interim Report of the Governor's Commission on School Construction (released April 15th) speaks to this very concern. One strategy the commission highlights as a potential solution is requiring "districts to contribute funds, rather than the existing all-or-nothing state funding approach, could increase capacity for more projects. Increased local contribution could be offset in part by reducing upfront planning costs via additional state-level technical assistance. Various options should be considered, including a sliding scale based on district characteristics or the incorporation of an approach similar to the SRRF."
L.D. 1087 attempts to correct some of these equity concerns in the school construction process - something our school leaders wholeheartedly support. However, it would not solve the broader issue of the lack of adequate resources to handle Maine's school construction needs. Maine's school infrastructure is decaying quickly, and more funding is badly needed. State officials say that conservatively, the cost to modernize Maine's aging schools would be $11 billion. This must be addressed if we are to make meaningful progress on this issue.
Currently, the Governor's Commission on School Construction is taking a broader look at all of these questions, and we would encourage your committee to wait to see the final Commission Report before passing any legislation.
